title: A prayer that isn't hers
hookLine: Christ has no body now but yours is widely credited to Teresa but doesn't appear in her writings

lines: CHRIST HAS NO BODY NOW BUT YOURS.
cards: A bookmark in a parish gift shop. A poster in a hospital chapel. A slide at the end of a volunteer training.
The words are lovely: Christ has no body now on earth but yours, no hands but yours, no feet but yours. And underneath, in small italic letters, a name: Teresa of Ávila.
It's a prayer people print, frame and read aloud at funerals. There's only one problem with the name at the bottom, and someone who loves Teresa might care about it.

teach.b: The lines don't appear in Teresa's writings. Readers have looked through her Life, The Way of Perfection, The Interior Castle, her Foundations and her letters, and the prayer isn't there.
Where it did come from isn't settled. So the name on the bookmark is a guess that hardened into a label. Does that make the prayer bad?

teach.h: THE IDEA IS PAUL'S: THE BODY OF CHRIST.
teach.b: Its idea runs straight back to Saint Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now you are the body of Christ, and members of member." Catholics can treasure the thought and use it. The only thing wrong is the signature.

teach.h: A VERSE TRADITION TIES TO HER.
teach.b: Now compare a short verse that tradition does connect with her. It was found, the story goes, in her breviary, the book she prayed from, written in Spanish.
It begins, let nothing disturb you, let nothing frighten you, and it ends, God alone is enough. Same saint, two paths to us: one with a trail you can follow, one without. Why care?
Because a saint's real voice is worth hearing on its own terms. Teresa's own writing can be funny, sharp and demanding in ways a gift-shop quote is not.

teach.h: CHECKING IS A WAY OF HONORING.
teach.b: And Scripture itself praises checking. The book of Acts describes the people of Berea, who heard Paul gladly but went home "daily searching the scriptures, whether these things were so."

teach.h: PROVE ALL THINGS; HOLD FAST THAT WHICH IS GOOD.
teach.b: Paul tells another church: "prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Checking a source isn't cynicism. It's a way of taking the words, and the person, seriously.

how: Catholics who study the saints read their words in critical editions of their writings, and Carmelite scholars note which popular sayings attributed to Teresa are not found there.

games.q: what does “a prayer that isn't hers” mean?
o: a good prayer, wrongly signed with Teresa's name
a prayer Teresa copied word for word from Paul
a prayer Teresa wrote but kept hidden from her nuns

p: Christ has no body now but yours
the verse tied to her breviary

s: Christ has no body now but yours appears in Teresa's Life
it doesn't appear in her writings, and where it came from isn't settled.
the idea behind the prayer goes back to Saint Paul
"now you are the body of Christ, and members of member."
checking a quote's source means you think it's a bad quote
the prayer's idea is good. only the signature is wrong.

games.q: you're one of the Bereans. a traveling preacher named Paul has just told you something new. what do you do?
o: accept it on the spot because he sounds sure.
hear it gladly, then search the scriptures to see if it's so.
games.why: Acts says they received the word eagerly and searched the scriptures daily, "whether these things were so." Acts praises them for it.

practice: Bring to mind a line you love, from a saint, a song, a poster, a parent, and ask yourself honestly: where do I know it from, and who actually said it?
If you pray, thank God for the words, whoever first wrote them; if you don't, just hold the line and the question together.

wordCard.voice: A prayer that isn't hers. Christ has no body now but yours: a good thought, rooted in Paul, but not found in Teresa's writings. Today's word.

orig.note: Spanish: God alone is enough. the closing line of the short verse tradition says was found in Teresa's breviary.

carryVoice: Your line: check the source. A good thought can stand without a borrowed name. See you tomorrow.
